annotation_target.structure: A simple strophic hymn form — the same melody repeating for each verse — confirmed by two small exact-repeat pairs late in the piece (measures 62/66 and 63/67, both four measures apart), consistent with a repeated final cadential phrase across the last two verses. Chord-window analysis reads the piece's harmonic home as Eb major — the basis for correcting the G major label this transcription originally carried: the opening labeled measures trace a clean Eb major-Ab major-Bb major-Eb major-Ab major-Eb major (I-IV-V-I-IV-I) hymn cadence at measures 2, 4, 8, 10, 12, and 13, followed by C minor (vi) at measure 14 — textbook hymn harmony, just centered on Eb rather than G. The opening is markedly sparse (measures 1, 3, 6, 7, and 8 all sit at 1-2 onsets), and the left hand doesn't fully establish itself until after a 4-measure gap around measures 6-9, giving the melody room to stand alone before the harmony fills in underneath it.
key_moments: Measures 1, 3, 6, 7, and 8 are the sparsest in the piece (1-2 onsets each) — the hymn opens almost bare, which demonstrates how much a melody can carry on its own before any accompaniment fills in.

Measures 6-9, a 4-measure gap in the left hand: the accompaniment steps back here, leaving the melody essentially unaccompanied for a full phrase. A chord window mid-gap, at measure 8, still reads Bb major — the dominant of the piece's Eb center, not the D that the original G major label would predict — and support fully resumes at measure 10, landing right back on the Eb tonic.
Measure 25 is the busiest in the piece (19 onsets) — the first real climax, arriving well into the piece rather than at the opening.

Measures 62/66 and 63/67 are exact repeats four measures apart — the final verse's cadential phrase echoing the one before it. The surrounding closing measures (58-69) read F major and Bb major in the chord windows — a dominant-preparation cadence in the piece's Eb center, not the G-D-G motion the original G major label would predict — a natural word-painting example for 'was blind, but now I see.'
The right hand's highest note, F6, arrives at measure 50 — in the second half of the piece, marking the melody's registral high point well after the hymn has fully established itself.
teaching_goals: Pentatonic/gapped-scale melody: learn to recognize how the tune avoids stepwise half-step motion in its most memorable phrases — that gapped quality is what gives it its folk, rather than strictly hymnal, character.
Unaccompanied phrasing: practice measures 6-9 with real rubato, since the left hand steps back and leaves the melody to carry the phrase alone.
Dynamic arc across a strophic form: with the real climax not arriving until measure 25, practice restraint in the opening verses so later verses have somewhere to grow.

Simple triple-meter hymn accompaniment over the Eb-Ab-Bb changes (I-IV-V — chord-window analysis reads this clearly; the G-C-D of the original G major label never appears): practice a bass note on beat 1 and a chord on beats 2-3 — the most basic hymn-accompaniment pattern, appropriate to this piece's spare character.
style_tips: Play the opening measures genuinely quiet and unhurried — this is not a piece to fill in with extra notes or rubato flourishes; the sparseness is the point.
Give the left-hand gap at measures 6-9 real space — resist the urge to fill it with a busier accompaniment than the arrangement calls for.
Try holding back through the opening verses rather than treating every verse at the same volume — a hymn like this earns its measure-25 climax through restraint beforehand.
Think of a hymn sung by a full congregation, not a solo showpiece — keep the tone warm and unforced, more communal than virtuosic.
